question.text: Is nasogastric decompression useful in prevention of leaks after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy?
question.context: Although its excellent results, laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG) presents major complications ranging from 0% to 29%. Among them, the staple line leak presents an incidence varying from 0% to 7%. Many trials debated about different solutions in order to reduce leaks' incidence. No author has investigated the role of gastric decompression in the prevention of this complication. Aim of our work is to evaluate if this procedure can play a role in avoiding the occurrence of staple line leaks after LSG. Between January 2008 and November 2012, 145 patients were prospectively and randomly included in the study. Seventy patients composed the group A, whose operations were completed with placement of nasogastric tube; the other 75 patients were included in the group B, in which no nasogastric tube was placed. No statistical differences were observed between group A and group B regarding gender distribution, age, weight, and BMI. No intraoperative complications and no conversion occurred in both groups. Intraoperative blood loss (50.1 ± 42.3 vs. 52.5 ± 37.6 ml, respectively) and operative time (65.4 ± 25.5 vs. 62.6 ± 27.8 min, respectively) were comparable between the two groups (p: NS). One staple line leak (1.4%) occurred on 6th postoperative day in group A patients. No leak was observed in group B patients. Postoperative hospital stay was significantly longer in group A vs. group B patients (7.6 ± 3.4 vs. 6.2 ± 3.1 days, respectively, p: 0.04).

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study found a significantly lower incidence of staple line leaks in the group that did not receive nasogastric decompression (Group B) compared to the group that did (Group A). This suggests that nasogastric decompression may be a useful tool in preventing staple line leaks after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: No leak was observed in group B patients.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While other factors could contribute to staple line leaks, the study design and the significant difference in leak rates between the two groups strongly suggest that nasogastric decompression plays a role in prevention.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study found no significant difference in staple line leak incidence between the two groups, with only one leak occurring in group A despite the use of nasogastric decompression. The p-value for the difference in hospital stay was 0.04, but this was not the primary outcome of interest. Given the lack of evidence supporting the effectiveness of nasogastric decompression in preventing leaks, the answer is no.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: No leak was observed in group B patients, while one leak occurred in group A despite the use of nasogastric decompression.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Other factors such as surgical technique, surgeon experience, and patient characteristics were not mentioned as different between groups, so they were not considered differentials.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study found no leak in the group without nasogastric decompression (Group B) versus one leak in the group with decompression (Group A), suggesting decompression may not prevent leaks and may even be associated with longer hospital stays. The lack of statistical difference in leak rates and the longer stay in Group A indicate no clear benefit.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: No leak was observed in group B (no nasogastric tube) versus one leak in group A (with nasogastric tube), with a statistically significant longer hospital stay in group A.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Considered whether decompression might reduce leak risk, but the data show no leak in the control group and a leak in the intervention group, making 'no' the best answer. Other factors like age, BMI, and operative time were balanced, reducing confounding.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: The possibility that other preventive measures or factors (not described in the case) may have contributed to the lower leak rate in group A, and the absence of a true control group makes it impossible to determine causality. Alternative decompression methods or standard care protocols were not compared, so the benefit of nasogastric decompression cannot be proven from this data alone.
